books.section: Topic 7.3 The Spanish-American War and Its Aftermath

primary_sources: President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898
Enrique Dupuy de Lôme, letter to José Canalejas, February 1898

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Spanish-American War marked a turning point in the United States' role in the world.

documents.title: McKinley's war message
documents.source: President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898. Paraphrased, with one short verbatim phrase.
documents.sourcing: McKinley, the president who had held back from war, asking Congress to authorize intervention in Cuba. A public appeal meant to gather votes, not a private doubt.
documents.text: McKinley gave Congress four reasons to intervene in Cuba. First, he said, was humanity: to end the barbarities, bloodshed, starvation, and horrible miseries in Cuba. Second was protection for American citizens in Cuba. Third was the serious injury to American commerce and trade. Fourth was that the war in Cuba was a constant menace to American peace.

documents.title: The de Lôme letter
documents.source: Enrique Dupuy de Lôme, Spanish minister to the United States, private letter to José Canalejas, February 1898. Translated excerpt; published in the New York Journal, February 9, 1898.
documents.sourcing: De Lôme, Spain's minister in Washington, writing privately to José Canalejas, editor of El Heraldo in Madrid. The letter was stolen by Cuban revolutionaries and printed by Hearst's Journal, so a private insult became a public one.
documents.text: "Besides the natural and inevitable coarseness with which he repeats all that the press and public opinion of Spain has said of Weyler, it shows once more what McKinley is: weak and catering to the rabble, and, besides, a low politician, who desires to leave a door open to me and to stand well with the jingoes of his party."

documents.title: The wreck of the Maine
documents.source: Detroit Photographic Co. photochrom, copyright 1900, Library of Congress cph.3g03933. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A commercial photochrom sold to the public two years after the explosion. The wreck was still sitting in Havana harbor, so the image shows how the incident stayed visible long after the war.
documents.text: The photograph shows the wrecked battleship USS Maine sitting low in the water of Havana harbor, its hull twisted and broken with one tall mast still standing. Small boats float nearby, and the Havana waterfront stands across the harbor behind it.

documents.title: The Teller Amendment
documents.source: Joint resolution of Congress, approved April 20, 1898. Public domain (abridged).
documents.sourcing: Congress, declaring the terms on which the United States would go to war. The amendment was a promise to the public and to Cuba that the war was for freedom, not for land.
documents.text: "First. That the people of the Island of Cuba are, and of right ought to be, free and independent. . . . Fourth. That the United States hereby disclaims any disposition or intention to exercise sovereignty, jurisdiction, or control over said Island except for the pacification thereof, and asserts its determination, when that is accomplished, to leave the government and control of the Island to its people."

documents.title: The Treaty of Paris
documents.source: Treaty of Peace between the United States and Spain, signed December 10, 1898. Public domain (abridged).
documents.sourcing: The peace treaty that ended the war, written by the victors. It records what the United States kept, not what it promised at the start.
documents.text: "Article I. Spain relinquishes all claim of sovereignty over and title to Cuba. Article II. Spain cedes to the United States the island of Porto Rico and other islands now under Spanish sovereignty in the West Indies, and the island of Guam in the Marianas or Ladrones. Article III. Spain cedes to the United States the archipelago known as the Philippine Islands. . . ." The United States agreed to pay Spain $20 million for the Philippine Islands.

documents.title: Aguinaldo protests American rule
documents.source: Emilio Aguinaldo, Second Proclamation, January 5, 1899. Translated excerpt.
documents.sourcing: Aguinaldo, president of the revolutionary government, protesting General Otis's claim to rule the Philippines. He speaks for Filipinos who had fought Spain and expected independence, not a new master.
documents.text: "I protest one and a thousand times, with all my energy in my soul, against such an authority. I solemnly proclaim that I have never had, either at Singapore or at Hongkong or here in the Philippines, any verbal or written contract for the recognition of American sovereignty over this cherished soil."

documents.title: The Platt Amendment
documents.source: Platt Amendment, Army Appropriations Act, approved March 2, 1901. Public domain (abridged).
documents.sourcing: Congress, setting the terms on which American troops would leave Cuba. Cuba had to write these terms into its own constitution, so the amendment shows who set the conditions of independence.
documents.text: "Article III. The Government of Cuba consents that the United States may exercise the right to intervene for the preservation of Cuban independence, the maintenance of a government adequate for the protection of life, property, and individual liberty, and for discharging the obligations with respect to Cuba imposed by the Treaty of Paris on the United States. . . . Article VII. . . . the Government of Cuba will sell or lease to the United States lands necessary for coaling or naval stations. . . ."

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the Spanish-American War marked a turning point in the United States' role in the world, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the closing of the western frontier, the European scramble for empire, or the search for markets after the Panic of 1893.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about the war as a turning point.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the annexation of Hawaii in 1898, the Insular Cases of 1901, or the Philippine-American War of 1899 to 1902.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of the turning point, explaining why the war changed some things and not others, or connecting the war to later American foreign policy.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The Spanish-American War was a turning point in the United States' role in the world: before 1898 America expanded across its own continent, and after 1898 it ruled overseas colonies, yet the turn was incomplete, because the republic kept arguing about whether empire betrayed its own ideals.
Context: After 1890 the frontier was closing, European powers were carving up Africa and Asia, and the Panic of 1893 left American factories searching for markets, so the question of what America should do abroad was suddenly urgent.
Evidence: Documents 1-3 show the war's causes — McKinley's humanitarian and commercial case, the de Lôme insult, and the Maine wreck that kept the incident before the public. Document 4 shows the war's stated aim, a free Cuba. Documents 5-7 show the outcome: the treaty kept the Philippines, Aguinaldo protested the new rule, and the Platt Amendment left Cuba independent in name only.
Beyond the documents: Hawaii was annexed in 1898, the Philippine-American War lasted three years and cost more than 4,000 American lives, and the Insular Cases of 1901 let the United States rule colonies without full constitutional rights.
Sourcing: McKinley speaks as a president gathering votes; de Lôme writes a private letter that became a public insult; Aguinaldo speaks as a revolutionary who expected independence; the Platt Amendment is Congress setting terms Cuba had to accept.
Complexity: The turn was real — America kept the colonies — but the Teller Amendment's promise and the Platt Amendment's limits show the country could not decide whether it was freeing peoples or ruling them.
